Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 54, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):

Surat al-Qamar

It is also called "Iqtarabat" (The Hour Has Drawn Near). It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that in the Torah it is called "al-Mubayyida" (the Whitener), because it whitens the face of its reciter on the Day when faces turn black. Al-Bayhaqi narrated it from him in Shu'ab al-Iman, but said: "It is munkar" (rejected, a weak report). "It is Meccan" according to the majority opinion. It was also said that it was revealed at the Battle of Badr. Muqatil said: "It is Meccan except for three verses," namely ﴿Or do they say...﴾ up to ﴿and bitterer﴾ [al-Qamar: 44-46]. Some limited the exception to ﴿The multitude will be routed﴾ [al-Qamar: 45], etc. This is refuted by what Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "Allah the Exalted revealed to His Prophet ﷺ in Mecca, before the Day of Badr, ﴿The multitude will be routed and they will turn their backs﴾."

"Umar ibn al-Khattab said: I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, which multitude will be routed?' When the Day of Badr came and the Quraysh were routed, I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ pursuing them with his sword drawn, and he was saying: ﴿The multitude will be routed and they will turn their backs﴾. So it was for the Day of Badr."

In al-Durr al-Manthur: al-Bukhari narrated from 'Aisha, who said: "It was revealed to Muhammad ﷺ in Mecca while I was a young girl playing: ﴿Nay, the Hour is their appointed time, and the Hour is more calamitous and bitter﴾ [al-Qamar: 46]." This, and what precedes it, refutes what is related from Muqatil as well. It was also said that the exception is only the two verses ﴿Indeed, the righteous﴾ [al-Qamar: 45]... Its verses are fifty-five by consensus. The connection between its beginning and the end of the preceding surah is evident, for He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Then the Approaching Calamity has drawn near﴾ [al-Najm: 57], and here ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾ [al-Qamar: 1]. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti said: The fine harmony in the sequence of these two surahs is not hidden, in terms of the correspondence in their names, due to the closeness between al-Najm and al-Qamar. Also, this one comes after that one, like al-A'raf after al-An'am, like al-Shu'ara' after al-Furqan, and like al-Saffat after Ya-Sin, in that it details the situations of the nations whose destruction was mentioned in His saying: ﴿And that He destroyed the first 'Ad﴾ ﴿and Thamud, He spared none﴾ ﴿and the people of Noah﴾ [al-Najm: 50], up to His saying: ﴿and the overturned cities He hurled down﴾ [al-Najm: 53].

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾, i.e., it has drawn very near. ﴿And the moon has split﴾: it was split, one part separating from another and becoming two halves. This occurred in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, about five years before the Hijrah. It is authentically reported from the narration of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and Ibn Jarir, from Anas, that the people of Mecca asked him, upon him be prayers and peace, to show them a sign, so he showed them the moon split into two, until they saw Hira' between them.

The report of Abu Nu'aym through the route of al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, that the rabbis of the Jews asked for a sign, so Allah the Exalted showed them the moon split, is not to be relied upon. In the two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud: "The moon split in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ into two halves: one half upon the mountain and one half beyond it. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Bear witness.'" And also from his hadith: "The moon split in the time of the Messenger of Allah, upon him be prayers and peace. The Quraysh said: 'This is the sorcery of Ibn Abi Kabshah.' A man said: 'Wait for what the travellers will bring you, for Muhammad cannot bewitch all the people.' The travellers came and informed them of that." Narrated by Abu Dawud and al-Tayalisi.

In the narration of al-Bayhaqi: "They asked the travellers, who had come from every direction, and they said: 'We saw it.'" Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split﴾.

Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, through a weak route, who said: "The polytheists gathered in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, among them al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, al-'As ibn Wa'il, al-'As ibn Hisham, al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, Rabi'ah ibn al-Aswad, and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. They said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'If you are truthful, split the moon for us into two halves: half over Abu Qubays and half over Qaynuqa'.' The Prophet ﷺ said to them: 'If I do, will you believe?' They said: 'Yes.' It was the night of the full moon. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked his Lord, mighty and majestic, to give him what they asked. The moon in the evening appeared split, half over Abu Qubays and half over Qaynuqa', while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called out: 'O Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Asad! O al-Arqam ibn al-Arqam! Bear witness.'"

The sound hadiths about the splitting are numerous, and scholars differed on whether it is mutawatir (widely transmitted). It was said: it is not mutawatir. In Sharh al-Mawaqif al-Sharifi, it is stated that it is mutawatir, and this is what al-'Allamah Ibn al-Subki chose. He said in his commentary on Ibn al-Hajib's Mukhtasar: "In my view the correct position is that the splitting of the moon is mutawatir, explicitly mentioned in the Qur'an, and reported in the two Sahihs and others through many diverse routes, so that there is no doubt about its being mutawatir," concluded in brief. Its hadiths have come in authentic narrations from a group of the Companions, among them 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, Anas, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Hudhayfah, Jubayr ibn Mut'im, Ibn 'Umar, and others. Yes, some of them did not witness it, such as Ibn 'Abbas, for he had not yet been born at that time, and such as Anas, for he was four or five years old in Medina. This does not undermine the soundness of the report, as is not hidden.

It occurs in the narration of al-Bukhari and others from Ibn Mas'ud: "We were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at Mina, and the moon split." This does not contradict what is authentically reported from Anas that it happened in Mecca, because he did not state explicitly that the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, was in Mecca that night. The meaning is that the splitting occurred while the Prophet ﷺ was residing in Mecca before he migrated to Medina.

In the Nazm al-Sirah of the Hafiz Abu al-Fadl al-'Iraqi there is a text explicitly affirming that the splitting occurred twice, and it is apparent that he regarded this as agreed upon, where he said: "And it split twice, by consensus." The basis of the first is perhaps what 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated through Mujahid, from Abu Ma'mar, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "I saw the moon split into two halves twice in Mecca, before the emergence of the Prophet ﷺ," the hadith continuing. As for consensus, it is not accepted. In al-Mawahib, al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said: "I think his saying 'by consensus' relates to 'split', not to 'twice', for I do not know of any scholar of hadith who asserted a multiplicity of splittings during his time ﷺ. Perhaps the one who said 'twice' meant 'two halves'. This is the only interpretation that seems appropriate, reconciling the reports," concluded. It is not hidden that this interpretation, despite its remoteness, does not fit the report of Ibn Mas'ud mentioned just above, because of the phrase "two halves" and "twice" together. My own view on the interpretation of this is that "twice" in Ibn Mas'ud's words qualifies the seeing, and multiplicity of seeing does not require multiplicity of the splitting, such that he saw it split, then turned his gaze away, then returned and saw it still in the same state, unchanged. This indicates that it was a seeing without any doubt. The disbelievers did something similar: Abu Nu'aym narrated through 'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The people of Mecca came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'Is there any sign by which we may know that you are the Messenger of Allah?' Gabriel descended and said: 'O Muhammad, tell the people of Mecca to gather this night, and they will see a sign.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ informed them of Gabriel's statement. They went out on the fourteenth night, and the moon split into two halves, one half over al-Safa and one half over al-Marwah. They looked, then rubbed their eyes, then looked again, then rubbed their eyes again, then looked, and said: 'This is nothing but sorcery.' So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split﴾." So if one of these had said, "I saw the moon split three times," in the sense of multiplicity of seeing, it would be correct without any doubt, and it would not require multiplicity of splitting. Thus the statement of Ibn Mas'ud should be interpreted in this manner, in order to reconcile the reports. Furthermore, this hadith, if authentic, is evidence for what al-Busayri indicated in his saying:

"His chest was opened, and the full moon was split for him, and every condition has a consequence."

That is, that the splitting occurred on the fourteenth night, because the full moon (al-badr) is the moon on the fourteenth night. From this one learns what al-'Allamah Ibn Hajar al-Haytami said in his commentary: "The apparent expression 'al-badr' rather than 'al-qamar' indicates that the splitting occurred on the fourteenth night, and I have found no predecessor for this." Perhaps he meant by "al-badr" the moon in general. What supports that it was the night of the full moon is what al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated through 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The moon eclipsed in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and they said: 'The moon has been bewitched.' So ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾ down to ﴿continuous﴾ was revealed." For an eclipse, although by custom it may occur on the thirteenth or fifteenth night, the more common case is the fourteenth night. There is no necessity to interpret the eclipse in this report as the splitting, since there is no impediment, as stated in al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, that the moon might have experienced an eclipse together with its splitting. Yes, it mentioned there that the context of this report is strange.

Furthermore, after its splitting, the moon's two parts did not leave the sky; rather they remained in it, separated by a distance for a moment, and then joined together. As for what some storytellers mention, that it entered the sleeve of the Prophet ﷺ and came out of his sleeve, this is false and has no basis, as related by Shaykh Badr al-Din al-Zarkashi from his teacher 'Imad ibn Kathir. May the curse of Allah the Exalted be upon the one who fabricated it. And what is in the report of Abu Nu'aym, which he narrated through al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, that it split and became two moons, one on al-Safa and the other on al-Marwah, for a period between the 'Asr and the night, while they looked at it and then it set, is not to be relied upon. How could it be, when that report includes that the splitting occurred at the request of the rabbis of the Jews, and that the speakers of "this is continuous sorcery" were them, which contradicts what the numerous authentic reports affirm, as is not hidden to one who investigates. And it has become widespread that "the Prophet ﷺ pointed at the moon with his blessed index finger and it split," but I have not found this in any authentic report. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

Al-Falasifa (the philosophers) denied that the splitting had actually occurred, on the basis of their claim that tearing and rejoining are impossible for the celestial bodies. Their proof for this is weaker than a spider's web, and it has been torn apart by the slightest breath of the thoughts of the People of Truth among the heavenly-minded, a tear that does not admit rejoining, as has been explained in its proper place. Some of the heretics (al-malahida) said: "If it had happened, it would have been transmitted by mass transmission (tawatur), and all the people of the earth would have shared in knowing it, and it would not have been confined to the people of Mecca, because it is a perceptible, observable matter in which people are equal. Human natures are eager to narrate the strange and to transmit what is unfamiliar. Nothing is stranger than the splitting of this great body, which was never known at all in ancient times. Had it had any basis, it would have been recorded in the books of astrology (al-tasyir) and astronomy (al-tanjim), and the astronomers (ahl al-irsad) would have mentioned it, since these sciences existed long before the Prophethood. Their unanimous abandonment of it and their neglect of it, despite its great importance and the clarity of the matter, is something custom does not permit." Also, it is not conceivable what cause could split this great body. Moreover, its splitting would produce a tremendous sound, far more violent than the sounds of destructive thunderbolts by manifold multiples, and the destruction of most of the people of the earth from it would not be far-fetched. Furthermore, once it was split and became two pieces, the force of mutual attraction would have departed from it, like a mountain when it splits, so it would necessarily remain split, or at least remain so for many years.

The answer to this is that it happened at night, during a time of inattention, and it lasted a short while. Seeing the moon in one land does not necessitate seeing it in all lands, because of the necessary difference of horizons. The moon may be rising for one people while absent from another, and eclipsed for one people while not eclipsed for others. Concern with astronomy (al-irsad) was not then what it is today, and the inattention of its people for a moment is not improbable. The splitting does not alter its stations (manazil), nor change its course. The most that can be said is that in the eastern piece there arose a force of motion to catch up with its western sister. And what would prevent God Most High from creating in it a speed like that which God, glorified is He, created in the light of the sun? For the people of the New Wisdom (ahl al-hikma al-jadida) have said: between the earth and the sun there are three hundred and forty thousand farsakh (a farsakh being a unit of distance), and its light reaches the earth in eight minutes and thirteen seconds, so light travels seventy thousand farsakh in each second. It is not necessary that the cause of every event be known. Rather, many repeated and observed events have not been traced to their causes, such as the seeing of the stars as near despite their extreme distance; they have mentioned that they have not determined its cause. It suffices for this that they have not determined the cause of vision by the eye in reality. Were someone to inform them, supposing that they had no perception of the properties of sight, though it is a small piece of fat whose conditions are well known to the anatomists, they would have denied it in the extreme and rejected it utterly, and attributed it to madness.

As for one who accepts the influence of souls to the point that a person can strike another merely by looking at him and directing his soul toward him, he would not find it improbable that there is a cause of this kind. It is established regarding the evil eye (ishabat al-ayn) that some of the Bedouin, who have a true-striking eye, can split the hump of a she-camel into two halves, and sometimes an image of it is formed for him from sand; he looks at it and splits it, and its hump splits, though he has not seen the camel itself. All of this is by way of accommodation to the reasoning of others. Otherwise, the will of God Most High is sufficient for the splitting, and likewise for all miracles and supernatural events. Were there a cause for every event, an infinite regress (tasalsul) would follow, and the proofs have established its invalidity. The claim that the tearing necessarily produces a tremendous sound is disputed in the present matter. Likewise, the disappearance of attraction is also disputed, since bodies differ in their properties, so it does not follow that the body of the moon and the earth are one in these respects. It is possible that one of the two pieces was like a great mountain in relation to the earth; if it was lifted away from it by some compelling force, for example, the earth would draw it back to itself so long as it did not exceed the limit of its pull, according to what they claim. And one may stipulate, regarding that piece, that it does not exceed the limit of attraction. Moreover, we are in no need of all of this, after establishing possibility and the comprehensiveness of His power, mighty and majestic is He, and that He, glorified is He, does whatever He wills.

In sum, the denier has nothing but the sense of improbability, and he cannot bring a proof for the intrinsic impossibility, even if it had split. In such situations, improbability is close to madness for one who possesses a sound intellect. It is related from al-Hasan that he said: "This splitting [occurred] after the second blast," and the expression in the past tense indicates that its occurrence is certain. This was also related from Ata. What supports what has preceded, and what the majority hold, is the reading of Hudhayfa: "and the moon has split" (wa qad inshaqqa al-qamar), for the clause on this reading is a circumstantial clause (haliyya), which implies simultaneity with the drawing near of the Hour, and that the splitting occurred before the Day of Resurrection. Likewise His saying, exalted is He:

[Page 78]

﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away﴾. This implies that the splitting (infishaq) is a sign they saw and turned away from. Some people claim that the splitting of the moon is a metaphor for the splitting of darkness at its rising, just as dawn is called *falaq* (daybreak) when the darkness splits apart. The term "splitting" (infilaq) is sometimes used in place of "splitting" (infishaq), as in the verse of al-Nabigha:

*"When they turned their backs, with a clamour behind them, a caller called us at the splitting (shaqq) of dawn."*

Another claims that the meaning of "the moon has split" is that the matter became clear and manifest. Both claims are unreliable and should not be relied upon or given attention. I do not think that those who advance them, if they affirm the Hour, which is greater than the splitting, and acknowledge the Islamic creeds on which there is consensus, would do so except out of complete lack of understanding and clinging to doubts that are as thin as the edge of a thumama (a small plant). Nevertheless, the one who denies this is not declared a disbeliever on the basis of the lack of consensus on its being mass-transmitted (mutawatir) and the verse not being explicit about it. Expulsion from the religion is a grave matter, so caution is exercised in it more than in anything else. And Allah the Exalted is the Granter of success.

The apparent meaning of "the nearness of the Hour" is its very close temporal proximity, since everything that is coming is near, while the age of the world is long, and what remains compared to what has passed is a small thing. The Imam inclined to the view that it means its nearness in minds and perceptions. The essence of this is that it is possible in a near possibility, such that no one should deny it. The use of "nearness" (iqtiraab), even though it is a matter that is certain, is like the use of *la'alla* (perhaps) in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ [al-Ahzab: 63], even though the matter is known to Allah the Exalted. The splitting of the moon is a clear sign according to this nearness. According to the first view, it was said that it is a sign of the very possibility that the nearness of occurrence entails. It was also said that it is a sign of the nearness of occurrence and a miracle for the Prophet ﷺ, on the basis that Allah the Exalted informed in His earlier books that when the Hour drew near the moon would split, as a miracle. Both of these, as you see, [are weak].

Some chose that it is a sign of the truthfulness of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, in all that he says and conveys from his Lord, the Glorified, because it is a miracle for him ﷺ. From this are his claim to prophethood, his report of the nearness of the Hour, and other things. The word ﴿sign﴾ (*aayah*) is indefinite in the context of a conditional, so it is general. Thus the meaning is "And if they see every sign, they turn away" from reflecting upon it, so as to understand the manner of its indication and the height of its rank. ﴿And they say, "Magic"﴾, i.e., "This," or "It," i.e., what we see, "is magic." ﴿Continuous﴾ (*mustamirr*), i.e., consistent and lasting, which Muhammad, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, brings over the passage of time. It clearly indicates the succession of signs and the continuity of miracles.

Abu al-Aliyah and al-Dahhak said: "*mustamirr*" means firmly twisted and strong, from *mirrah* (with a fatha or kasra), meaning strength. It is originally the verbal noun of *marartu al-habl* (I twisted the rope), when I twisted it firmly. So by it is meant, figuratively and by a loose metonymy, anything firm.

Anas, Yaman, Mujahid, al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', and al-Nahhas (who chose it) said: *mustamirr* means passing, going away, quickly vanishing. By this they consoled themselves and entertained themselves with empty wishes, as though they said: "The state of him, peace and blessings be upon him, and the miracles that appeared through him, are a summer cloud that will soon disperse." ﴿But Allah refuses except to perfect His light, though the disbelievers dislike it﴾ [al-Tawbah: 32].

It was also said: "*mustamirr*" means extremely bitter, i.e., loathsome to us and repellent because of its intense bitterness. One says: *marra al-shay'* and *amarra* when a thing becomes bitter, and *amarra ghayrahu* and *marrahu* (both intransitive and transitive). It was also said: "*mustamirr*" resembles one another, i.e., its acts have continued in this manner of imaginings. It was also said: "*mustamirr*" passes from the earth to the heaven, i.e., his magic reached the point that it bewitched the moon. But this is nothing. Perhaps the most suitable [interpretation], given their extreme obstinacy and arrogance, is what was related from Anas and those with him.

It was also read as ﴿وإنْ يُرَوْا﴾ (*wa-in yuraw*), with the passive voice from *al-ira'ah* (showing).

﴿And they denied﴾ the Prophet ﷺ and what Allah the Exalted manifested through his hand of the signs, ﴿and followed their desires﴾, which Satan had made appealing to them. It was also said: "they denied" refers to the sign that is the splitting of the moon, ﴿and followed their desires﴾, and said: "The moon has been bewitched," or "our eyes have been bewitched, while the moon remains in its state." The conjunction (ʿaṭf) is upon the preceding conditional (jazāʾ), and the use of the past tense indicates certainty. It was also said: the conjunction is upon ﴿has drawn near﴾, and the conditional clause is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) to explain their habit when they witnessed signs. His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and every matter is settled﴾, is a new sentence (istiʾnāf) brought to refute the disbelievers in their denial, by explaining that there is no benefit for them in it, and that the exalted status of the Prophet ﷺ is not diminished by it; or it is said to despair them of what they hung their empty hopes upon, namely that his matter is not settled, as they said: ﴿a continuous magic﴾, by stating its firmness and permanence. That is, every matter among the matters reaches an end at which it will necessarily settle, and among them is the matter of the Prophet ﷺ, so it will arrive at an end at which its truth and the exaltedness of his status will become clear. And to indicate the manifestation of this end for his matter, peace and blessings be upon him, the verb of settling was not stated explicitly. In al-Kashshaf: that is, every matter must reach an end at which it settles, and his matter ﷺ will reach an end at which it becomes clear whether it is true or false, and the outcome for them will be made manifest to him. Or: every matter of his, peace and blessings be upon him, and of theirs, is settled, that is, it will be established and settle in a state of victory or abandonment in this world, or happiness or wretchedness in the Hereafter. Al-Kashf says: the statement according to the first view is a concluding remark (tadhyīl) functioning as a proverb, and according to the second it is a concluding remark that is not independent.

Shayba read "mustaqarrun" with a fatha on the qaf, and it is transmitted from Nafiʿ. Abu Hatim claimed that it has no basis, but it was explained as "mustaqarran" being a verbal noun (maṣdar) with the meaning of "istiqrār" (settling). Taking it as applying to "every matter" would require an implied noun, that is, "possessor of settlement," but even without this implied noun, if intensification is intended, it is valid. It was also permitted that it be a noun of time or place, with an implied noun as well, that is, "possessor of a time of settling," or "possessor of a place of settling." It was objected that the statement that every matter must have a time or a place is a known fact with no benefit in mentioning it, and it was answered that it establishes settling for it by way of metonymy (kināya), which is more eloquent than explicit statement.

Zayd ibn ʿAli read "mustaqirrin" with a kasra on the qaf and in the genitive case, and it was explained that it is an attribute of "amr" (matter), and that every item is conjoined to "the Hour," that is: "the Hour has drawn near, and every matter that settles and whose condition becomes clear has drawn near," that is, with its nearness. Al-Kashf says: in this there is a trace of abstraction (tajrīd) and a great awe-inspiring effect, in that it made in the drawing near of the Hour the drawing near of every matter that has a settled state and whose condition becomes clear, among those things that have an impact. His statement exalted is He: ﴿and the moon split﴾, according to this reading, is either with an implied "qad" (indicating certainty), which its recitation with "qad" supports, or it is treated as a digression (iʿrāḍ) since it confirms the nearness of the Hour. His statement, glorified is He: ﴿and if they see a sign﴾ etc., is a digression that arises from mentioning the splitting of the moon.

Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying it is remote because of the many intervening elements between the conjunct and the conjoined, and that making the speech of this kind is like: "I ate bread, and I struck Khalid, and if Zayd comes, honor him, and he set off toward the sons of So-and-so," and "meat" conjoined to "bread." He then said: rather, the like of it is not found in Arabic speech. It was answered that this is nothing, because when evidence indicates the conjunction, that is not considered a barrier to it; moreover, there is a difference between the verse and the example that is not hidden. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said that "mustaqarrun" is the predicate (khabar) of "kull" (every), and the genitive is by proximity (jiwār). Abu Hayyan also objected to this, saying it is not good, because genitive by proximity is extremely anomalous in such a case, since it is not known in the predicate of a subject, and it is known only in the attribute, with the grammarians differing over its existence. He preferred that "kull" be the subject (mubtadaʾ) with a predicate that is implied, like "āt" (coming), or a thing acted upon and the like, which the speech indicates, or that it is mentioned afterward, namely His statement exalted is He: ﴿wisdom far-reaching﴾. It has been objected to between them with His statement, glorified is He:

[Page 79]

﴿And certainly there has come to them﴾ in the Qur'an ﴿of the news﴾, i.e., the reports of the bygone generations, or the reports of the Hereafter. The prepositional phrase (al-jar wa'l-majrur) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "mā" in His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿wherein is a deterrent﴾. It is fronted before it for the sake of the verse-ending (al-fāṣila) and to give it emphasis (tatwīq ilayh). The "min" (min) is either partitive (lil-tab'īḍ) or explanatory (lil-tabyīn), based on the preferred view that it may precede what it explains. Al-Radi said: The explanatory "min" may precede the vague term in phrases such as "ʿindī min al-māl mā yakfī" (I have of the wealth what suffices), because it is originally a qualifier of an implied noun, i.e., "shayʾun min al-māl" (a thing of the wealth), and what is mentioned is an apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to the implied explicated noun preceding it, so that clarification comes after vagueness. That is: certainly there has come to them, being among the news, that which contains a deterrent for them and a restraint from the vile deeds in which they are engaged; or it is a place of deterrence and restraint, and these are the reports of punishment, or the reports of threat.

The root of ﴿muzdajar﴾ is *muztajar*, with the tā' (of the iftiʿāl form) placed after the zāy, and the tā' of iftiʿāl is changed to dāl (muzdajar) to harmonize with the following dāl, dhāl, or rāʾ. It has also been read *muzzajar*, with the tā' changed to zāy and the first zāy assimilated into the second. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read *muzjir*, an active participle from azjara, meaning "becoming one possessing a deterrent," like aʿshaba, "becoming one possessing grass." ﴿Wisdom consummate﴾, i.e., reaching the utmost degree of perfection, with no defect in it. ﴿Ḥikmatun﴾ is nominative, being either a substitution of the whole (badal kull) or of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) from "mā," and it has been said that it is from ﴿muzdajar﴾, or the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "hiya" (it is), or "hādhihi" (this is), with the demonstrative referring to what is implied by the discourse of the sending of messengers, the clarification of evidence, and the warning to those who passed, or to what is in the reports, or to the imminent Hour. The verse indicating it, as the Imam said and as was mentioned just before, is the possibility that it is a predicate about all of it in the reading of Zayd. Al-Yamani read *ḥikmatan bālighatan* in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "mā," for it is either a relative pronoun or an indefinite qualified noun. It is permissible for the circumstantial clause to come from it while being placed after it, or it is in the sense of "aʿnī" (I mean).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 54, verse 5:

﴿Then what use are the warnings?﴾ It is either a negation of benefit (ighna'), or an interrogative of denial (istifham inkari). The fa' (fa) indicates the sequence of the non-benefit upon the arrival of the far-reaching wisdom, even though it is the place where benefit is expected. The form of the present tense (al-mudari') indicates renewal and continuity. As for "ma" in the second aspect, it is in the accusative position as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), meaning: "What benefit do the warnings bring?" It has also been permitted that it be in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), with the sentence following it as its predicate (khabar), and the returning pronoun (al-'a'id) is implied, meaning: "What do the warnings bring him?" The word "nudhur" is the plural of "nadhir" in the sense of "the one who warns" (al-mundhir). It has also been permitted that it is the plural of "nadhir" in the sense of "warning" (al-indhar). This was objected to on the grounds that the proper rule for a verbal noun (masdar) is that it is not dualized or pluralized, and that it should be a verbal noun like "al-indhar." This was objected to on the grounds that this is contradicted by the feminine form of the verb attributed to it, and that its being taken in the sense of "nidharah" (warning) is not hidden in its state.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 54, verse 6:**

﴿So turn away from them.﴾ The *fa'* (الفاء) here indicates causation (*sababiyyah*), and what is caused is the turning away, or the command to turn away. The cause is their not being benefited by warnings, or the knowledge of that. By "turning away" is meant either not fighting them, in which case the verse is abrogated (*mansukhah*, meaning its ruling has been superseded), or leaving off disputation with them, in which case the verse is clear and unabrogated (*muhkamah*). The first meaning is the apparent one. ﴿On the day the caller calls﴾: the phrase *yawma* (يوم) is an adverbial of time (*zarf*) governed by *li-yakhruju* (لِيَخْرُجُونَ, "they will come out"), or it is an object (*maf'ul bihi*) of an implied *udhkur* (اذْكُرْ, "remember"). It has also been said that it is governed by *intazir* (انتظِرْ, "wait"). It is permissible for it to be an adverbial governed by *tughni* (تُغْنِي, "will avail"), or by an implied stative verb (*mustaqarr*), with what lies between them being a parenthetical interjection (*i'tiraD*). It is also permissible for it to be an adverbial governed by *yaqulu al-kafiru* (لِيَقُولَ الكافِرُ, "the disbeliever will say"), or by *tawalla* (لِتَوَلَّ, "turn away"), meaning: turn away from interceding for them on the Day of Resurrection. Or it may be an object of purpose (*ma'mul lahu*) with *ila* (إلى, "until") implied, and the saying of al-Hasan supports this: "So turn away from them until a day..."

The intended meaning is the continuation of the turning away, and all of these readings, as you see, are possible.

The caller is Israfil, peace be upon him. It has also been said that he is Jibril, peace be upon him, and it has been said that he is another angel entrusted with this task. It is permissible for the calling to be for the resurrection on that day, like the command in ﴿Be, and it is﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:117) and other verses, according to the view that it is a figure of speech (*tamthil*). In that case the caller is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The *waw* in *yad'u* (يَدْعُ) has been dropped in pronunciation because of the meeting of two unvocalised letters (*iltiqa' al-sakinayn*), and also dropped in the written form, following the pronunciation. The *ya'* in *al-da'i* (الداعِ) has been dropped for lightness, and the *alif-lam* (ألْ) has been treated as a substitute for tanwin (التنوين), since it replaces it. Something may be analysed by reference to its opposite just as it may be analysed by reference to its counterpart.

﴿To a dreadful thing﴾: *nukur* (نُكُرٍ) means terrible, a thing which souls find abhorrent because they have no precedent for its like, and this is the terror of the Resurrection. *Nukur* is used figuratively for the terrible, because what is usually strange (*munkar*) is something unfamiliar. It is also permissible for it to derive from *inkar* (الإنكار), the opposite of *iqrar* (acknowledgement). Whichever it is, it is an adjective of the pattern *fu'l* (فُعُل, with two *damma*s), which is rare among adjectives. Examples of this pattern include: *rawdah unuf lam tur'a* (a meadow untouched and unpastured), and *rajul shulul* (a man who is quick in responding to needs, quick, good in companionship, and of good disposition), and *sajh layyin sahl* (a smooth, gentle, easy-going [person]).

Al-Hasan, Ibn Kathir and Shibl read *nukr* (نُكْرٌ) with a sukun on the *kaf*, as in the saying *shughl* and *shughl* (شُغُلٌ وشُغْلٌ), and *usur* and *usr* (عُسُرٌ وعُسْرٌ). This is a lightened sukun, or the sukun is the original form and the *damma* was introduced for harmony with the preceding vowel (*al-ittiba'*). Mujahid, Abu Qilabah, al-Jahdari and Zayd ibn Ali read *nukira* (نُكِرَ) as a past-tense verb in the passive voice (*fi'l madi mabni lil-maf'ul*), meaning "he disapproved of," in the sense of *ankara* (أنكرَ, "he rejected").

*[Page 80]*

﴿with their eyes humbled﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the subject of ﴿they will come forth﴾, meaning they will come forth ﴿from the sepulchres﴾, i.e., the graves, with their eyes abased from the intensity of the terror; that is, they will be humbled because of it. The circumstantial clause was placed first for the flexibility (tasarruf) of the governing verb and for emphasis. In this there is evidence against the view of al-Jurmi that a circumstantial clause may not precede the verb, even when the verb is flexible. It is also refuted by their saying: "Scattered, the herd returns (shattā ta'ūbu al-ḥilbah)," and by his saying:

Swiftly does the hardship become easy for people of intellect, when with a true hope they face adversity.

It has been made a circumstantial clause of that, on the basis of His saying, Exalted: ﴿On the day they come forth from the sepulchres in haste﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 43], up to His saying: ﴿their eyes humbled﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 43–44]. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause from the omitted object pronoun in ﴿the caller calls﴾, i.e., the caller calls them. This has been criticised on the grounds that it does not conform to what was revealed, and also that it would become an anticipated circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddarah), because calling is not the state of the eyes' humbling, and it is not of the same multiplicity as the others. Likewise, it has been made the object of "he calls" with the meaning "he calls a group whose eyes are humbled," i.e., they will humble, although this is closer than what preceded it. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in the genitive in His saying: ﴿so turn away from them﴾, and there is in this what is not hidden.

﴿their eyes﴾ is the subject (fā'il) of ﴿humbled﴾, and the adjective agrees with it in the plural, because when it is a broken plural (jam' taksīr), it no longer resembles the verb in form, so agreement is good in it. This is unlike when it takes the sound masculine plural (jam' mudhakkar sālim), for its pattern does not change and it resembles the verb, so it should not be pluralised when it takes an apparent plural noun as its subject, according to the eloquent dialect, not the dialect of akalūnī al-barāghīth ("the fleas ate me"). However, pluralisation in that case is lighter in the noun than in the verb, as al-Radi said, and its reason is clear. In al-Tashil (the book of Ibn Malik), it is said: when an adjective takes an apparent plural noun as its subject, if it can be made a broken plural, as in marartu bi-rajulin qiyāmin ghilmānuhu ("I passed by a man, standing, whose boys..."), this is preferable to its singular form, as in marartu bi-rajulin qā'imin ghilmānuhu. This is the view of al-Mubarrad and those who followed him, and the usage supports it, as in his saying:

Standing over them were my companions, their mounts beside them, saying: "Do not perish from grief, but take courage."

And his saying:

With a straight, supple spear whose joints are true, and with a sharp, bright blade that cleaves the helmets.

The majority said: the singular is preferable, and analogy is with them, and upon it is his saying:

And men whose faces are handsome, from Iyad ibn Nizar ibn Ma'add.

It has also been said: if it follows a singular noun, the singular is preferable, as in rajulun qā'imun ghilmānuhu; and if it follows a plural noun, the plural is preferable, as in rijālun qiyāmun ghilmānuhum. As for the dual and the sound plural, they are on the dialect of akalūnī al-barāghīth. It is also permitted that in ﴿humbled﴾ there is a concealed pronoun, and that ﴿their eyes﴾ is a substitute (badal) for it. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Jahdari, Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿khāshi'an﴾ in the singular, while Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿khāshi'atan﴾ (feminine). It has also been read ﴿khushsha'un﴾, taking it as a predicate preceding its subject, with ﴿their eyes﴾ as the subject (mubtada'), and the sentence in the position of a circumstantial clause.

His saying, Exalted: ﴿as though they were scattered locusts﴾ is also a circumstantial clause. Their likeness to scattered locusts is in multitude, in surging, and in spreading across the horizons. Their likeness to scattered moths (farāsh mabthūth) has also come, and for them on the day of coming forth there is a share of resemblance to each. It has been said: at first they will be like moths when they surge in alarm, not knowing where to head, since moths have no direction they aim for; then they will be like scattered locusts when they head towards the gathering place. Thus the two comparisons refer to two different times. This has been related from Makki ibn Abi Talib.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 54, verse 8:

﴿Hastening towards the caller﴾ — rushing towards him. Abu 'Ubayda said: some added "stretching out their necks," and another "with trembling, fear and a fixed gaze."
Page 81
ʿIkrima said: "turning their ears towards the sound." It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: "gazing at him, their eyes not turning away from him." He cited the verse of Tubba':

"Namir ibn Sa'd serves me, and I see that Namir ibn Sa'd is obedient to me and hastening (muhti'un)."

In another report, he explained it as "humbled (khadi'in)" and cited the verse. It was also said: "lowering what is between their eyes." Sufyan said: "their eyes fixed upon the sky." It was also said: the origin of al-hat' (hasting with the neck stretched) is the stretching of the neck, or the stretching of the gaze, and then it is used metaphorically for hastening, or for looking and reflecting, so pay attention. ﴿The disbelievers say: This is a difficult day﴾ — hard, severe, because of what they witness of the signs of its terror and what they expect of the evil outcome awaiting them in it. Attributing this saying to the disbelievers contains an allusion that it is not so for the believers.

﴿Qawm Nuh kadhdhabat qablahum﴾ The people of Noah denied before them. This begins a list of some of the prophets mentioned, whose stories should prompt restraint, and it is a kind of elaboration of them. It also shows that they were not affected by warnings, confirming the implication of His, exalted is He, words: ﴿So the warnings avail nothing﴾. The verb is treated as intransitive, meaning: the people of Noah denied (the truth) before your people denied. His, exalted is He, words ﴿So they denied Our servant﴾ explain that undefined denial, as in His, exalted is He, words ﴿And Noah called out to his Lord and said﴾ [Hud: 45], and so on. This adds further confirmation and affirmation of the denial. It is also permissible that the meaning is: they denied repeatedly, one denial after another, so that whenever a denying generation passed away, another denying generation followed it. Or the meaning is: the people of Noah denied the Messengers, and so, since they denied the Messengers and rejected prophethood entirely, they denied Noah because he was one of the Messengers; the "fa" (so) in "fakadhdhabu" is then causal. It is also said: the meaning of "kadhdhabat" is that they intended denial and initiated it, and the meaning of "fakadhdhabu" is that they completed it and reached its end, as it was said in the verse: "And God mended the religion, so it was mended" (wa qad jabara al-din al-Ilah fa-jabar). Mentioning him, peace be upon him, by the title of servitude, with its attribution to the "nun of majesty" (the plural of majesty), exalts him, peace be upon him, elevates his station, and censures those who denied him.

﴿Wa qalu majnun﴾ That is, they did not limit themselves to mere denial, but attributed madness to him, saying: he is mad. ﴿Wa-zdujir﴾ is coordinated with "qalu" and is a report from Him, mighty and majestic. That is: he was restrained from conveying the message through various kinds of harm and intimidation. This is what Ibn Zayd said, and he recited: ﴿If you do not desist, O Noah, you will surely be among those stoned﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 116]. Mujahid said: it is part of their own statement, meaning: he is mad, and the jinn have overcome him, taken away his reason, and made him stagger. The first view is more evident and more eloquent. The verb is made passive for the sake of the fasilah (the rhyming verse-ending), and the tongues are spared from mentioning them, indicating that their act is worse than their statement.

﴿فَدَعا رَبَّهُ أنِّي﴾ That is, "that I".

Ibn Abi Ishaq, ʿIsa, al-Aʿmash, and Zayd ibn ʿAli read "إنِّي" with a kasra on the hamza, and it is also transmitted from ʿAsim. According to the Basrans, this is by supposing an implied verb of saying (idmar al-qawl). According to the Kufans, it is because the act of supplication is treated as equivalent to speech (ijra' al-duʿaʾ majra al-qawl). ﴿إنِّي مَغْلُوبٌ﴾ means: "I am overcome" (maghlub) by my people; I have no power to take vengeance on them. ﴿فانْتَصِرْ﴾ means: so avenge me against them. It has also been said that it means: so defend yourself, since they denied your messenger. It has also been said that what is meant by "maghlub" is that my soul overcame me, so that I invoked destruction upon them, but this is contrary to the apparent meaning. He (peace be upon him) did not invoke destruction upon them except after despair of their faith. The emphasis (al-taʾkid) is for greater attention to the matter of mercy (al-tarahhum), which is the intended purpose of the report.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 54, verse 11:

﴿So We opened the gates of heaven with water pouring forth.﴾ That is, pouring down (manṣabb). It was also said: abundant. The poet said:

"My eyes, pour forth tears in abundance
over the best of those who dwell, from Ma'add and those present."

The bāʾ (with) is for instrumentality, like its use in "I opened the door with the key." It is also permitted that it be for accompaniment (mulābasah), but the first is more eloquent. In the sentence there is a figurative metaphor (istiʿārah tamthīliyyah), by likening the flowing of rain from the clouds to the pouring of rivers by which the gates of heaven were opened and the hide of the green dome was split. This is what the majority (al-Jumhūr) held. Others held that it is to be taken in its literal sense, and this is the apparent meaning of the words of Ibn ʿAbbas.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him that he said: "The sky did not rain before that day or after it except from clouds; but on that day the gates of heaven were opened with water without clouds, and the two waters met." In another narration: "It did not cease for forty days." And from al-Naqqash that the gates were meant to be the Milky Way (al-Majarrah), which is the crack (sharaj) of the sky like the crack of a leather bag (ʿaybah)! What is known from astronomical observation, however, is that the Milky Way is a multitude of small stars very close to one another. And God knows best.

It is strange that they used to ask for rain for years, and God destroyed them by what they had asked for. Ibn ʿAmir, Abu Jaʿfar, al-Aʿraj and Yaʿqub read «fa-fattahnā» with the doubled letter (tashdīd) because of the multitude of gates. The apparent view is that the plural of paucity (jamʿ al-qillah) here denotes plurality.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 54, verse 12:**

﴿And We caused the earth to burst forth with springs﴾. And We made the entire earth as if it were gushing springs. Its original form was "We caused the springs of the earth to burst forth," and it was changed to the *tamyiz* (specification, an accusative noun clarifying a preceding ambiguity) for the sake of emphasis (*mubalagha*), by making the whole earth gushing, together with the ambiguity and its explanation. So the *tamyiz* is transferred from the object. Some scholars took it as transferred from the subject, on the basis that this is the more common case: the original would be "the springs of the earth gushed forth." Transferring it from the subject, as with transferring from the subject of the verb mentioned, can also be from the subject of another verb that corresponds to it in derivation, and this is one such case. This is an unnecessary strain, and there is no need for it. Some scholars prevented the *tamyiz* from coming from the object and so parsed ﴿springs﴾ as a deferred circumstantial clause (*hal muqaddara*). It is also permitted that it be a second object of *fajjarna* (We caused to burst), with *fajjarna* taken to imply a verb that governs a second object, meaning: "by the bursting We made the earth springs." According to some reports, this lasted forty days. ʿAbdullah and his companions, Abu Haywa, and al-Mufaddal from ʿAsim read "*fajarna*" with the lighter form. ﴿Then the waters met﴾, that is, the water of the sky and the water of the earth. The singular is used to affirm that the meeting of the two waters was not merely by adjacency but by mixing and merging. ʿAli, may God ennoble his face, al-Hasan, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb, and al-Jahdari read "*al-maʾani*" (the two waters) in the dual, in order to show the difference between the two kinds, though "*al-maʾ*" (the water) in the singular includes both the water of the sky and the water of the earth. A similar usage is the poet's saying:

*"For us are two camels, in which you know (what there is); so choose from whichever of them you wish, and turn away."*

It is said that there is an indication here that the water of the earth gushed forcefully and rose until it met the water of the sky, and this carries an emphasis not understood from the singular. Al-Hasan also read "*māwān*" (with a *waw*), by changing the hamza into a *waw*, like the form *ʿilbāwān* (a kind of tree), as al-Zamakhshari said. He did not mean that it is analogous to it, but rather that just as there is a substitution there, for the reason that it is non-original since it is an added letter for affixation (*ilhaq*), so also here, because it is a substitute. Although the substitution is from the *hāʾ*, it was treated as a substitute for the *waw*. He analogized it to the relative form (*nisba*), as stated in *al-Kashshaf*. It is also reported from him that the form is *"al-māyān"* with the hamza changed into a *yāʾ*.

﴿according to a matter that had been decreed﴾. That is, existing in a state that God Most High had determined from eternity without any variation, or in a state that was measured and arranged, namely that what descended was in proportion to what came out.

It is said that the water of the earth rose seventeen cubits, and the water of the sky descended to complete forty. It is also said that the water of the earth was greater, and it had a specific measure with God, may He be exalted. Or, "according to a matter that God had decreed and written in the Preserved Tablet," which is the destruction of the people of Noah by the Flood.

Abu Hayyan preferred this, on the ground that every story mentioned after the mention of God includes the destruction of the deniers, so this would be a metonymy for the destruction of these people. The "*ʿalā*" (according to) is for causation, and it is possible that it is connected to "*iltaqa*" (met). This contains a refutation of the astrologers, who claimed that the Flood occurred because the seven planets, other than Venus, were gathered in a watery sign. Abu Haywa and Ibn Muqsim read "*qudira*" with the *dal* doubled (*qaddara*).

[Page 83]

﴿And We carried him﴾, i.e., Noah, peace be upon him, ﴿upon [a vessel] of planks﴾, meaning broad pieces of wood, ﴿and nails﴾, i.e., nails (*masamir*), as said by the majority of scholars and by Ibn ʿAbbas in the narration of Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir. It is the plural of *disar*, like *kitab* and *kutub* (book and books). It was also said that *dusur* is like *saqf* and *suqf* (roof and roofs). The root meaning of *dasr* is a strong forceful push, so the nail was named after it, because it is struck and driven in with force. It was also said that *dusur* means ropes of palm fibre with which ships are fastened. Al-Layth said: they are threads with which their planks are tied together. ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from ʿIkrimah and al-Hasan that they are the prows of the ship and its front, which strikes the waves and pushes them away. A similar report is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. He also narrated from Mujahid that they are the crossbeams of the ship, that is, the pieces of wood laid across its middle.

In another narration from him, they are the ribs of the ship. Whatever the meaning, the words of the Exalted, ﴿possessing planks and nails﴾, are among the descriptive phrases that stand in place of the things described, by way of *kinaya* (metonymy, indirect reference). This is like their saying: "a living being, upright in stature and broad in nails," meaning a human being. It is among the eloquent and elegant forms of speech. A parallel to the verse is the statement of the poet:

"My bed is the saddle of a horse, but my shirt is chain mail of iron."

He meant by "my shirt" a coat of mail. And his saying, describing the emaciation of camels:

"Every eye sees her as a target, even in the eyes of the locusts that leap, with their hind legs."

He meant "in the eyes of locusts," because leaping on the hind legs is specific to them. As for whether the word described is omitted, with the attribute indicating it, as stated in *al-Mufassal* and elsewhere, that is a matter of grammar.

﴿تَجْرِي بِأعْيُنِنا﴾ [sailing under Our eyes], meaning in Our sight. It is a metaphor for protection, i.e., it sails on that water under Our guarding and Our care. It was also said: "with Our protégés," meaning Noah (peace be upon him) and those who believed with him. It is said: "a 'eye' (ʿayn) of Allah the Exalted, or one of His protégés (awliyāʾ), may He be glorified." It was also said: "with eyes," meaning the waters that We caused to gush forth. It was also said: "with the guardian angels (ḥafaẓa), peace be upon him," whom He called "eyes" and attributed to Himself, may His majesty be exalted. The first explanation is the most apparent. Zayd ibn ʿAlī and Abū al-Sammāl read بِأعْيُنّا with idgham (assimilation, merging of the two identical consonants).

﴿جَزاءً لِمَن كانَ كُفِرَ﴾ [as a recompense for one who had been disbelieved], meaning: Our doing that is a recompense for Noah (peace be upon him), for he was a blessing that Allah the Exalted bestowed upon his people, but they disbelieved in it. Likewise, every prophet is a blessing from Allah the Exalted upon his community. It is also permissible that it be read with the preposition omitted, the verb reaching the pronoun, and the pronoun concealed within the verb after it has been changed to the passive (mabnī lil-majhūl)—meaning: "for one who was disbelieved in," that is, Noah (peace be upon him) as well, meaning his prophethood was denied. In this case, kufr (disbelief) toward him is the opposite of faith. According to the first reading, it is kufr al-niʿmah (ingratitude for a blessing). It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid that the one intended is Allah the Exalted, as if it were said: "in anger and in victory for Allah, mighty and majestic." This, as you see, is far-fetched.

Maslama ibn Muḥārib read كَفْرَ with the fāʾ sukūn, the lightened form of faʿala (mukhaffaf faʿala, the lightened verb pattern), as in the line of poetry:

"Were the willow-ban and musk pressed out of him, he would be pressed out."

Yazīd ibn Rūmān, Qatādah and ʿĪsā read كَفَرَ in the active voice (mabnī lil-fāʿil), and then the one intended is only the people of Noah (peace be upon him). In this reading there is evidence for the occurrence of the past tense as the predicate of kāna without qad. This is the view of the Basrans and others, whereas they (the others) say that qad must appear, either explicitly or implicitly. It is also permissible that kāna be redundant (zāʾidah), as if it were said: "as a recompense for one who disbelieved and did not believe."

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 54, verse 15:**

﴿And We left it﴾, i.e., We preserved the ship ﴿as a sign﴾. This is based on what is narrated from Qatada and al-Naqqash, that its timber remained on al-Judi until some of the earliest people of this community saw it. Or it means: We preserved its account. Or: We preserved its kind, namely by preserving ships. Or, with ﴿taraknaha﴾ taken in the sense of "We made it": it is also permitted for the pronoun to refer to the event, which is the deliverance of Nuh (peace be upon him) and those with him, and the drowning of the disbelievers. ﴿So is there anyone who will take heed?﴾, i.e., one who takes admonition from that sign, being deserving of taking heed.

Qatada, as transmitted by Ibn 'Atiyya, read ﴿muddakir﴾ with the dhal pointed (مُذَّكِّرٍ), by converting the ta' of the ifti'al form (ta' al-ifti'al, the infixed ta' of the reflexive verb form) into a dhal and assimilating (idgham) the dhal into the dhal. The author of al-Lawami' said: Qatada read ﴿fa-hal min muddhakir﴾ (فَهَلْ مِن مُذَكِّرٍ) with a doubled kaf, from al-tadhkir (admonition), meaning: one who reminds himself or others by it. It is also read as مُذْتَكِرٍ, with a dotted dhal followed by the ta' of the ifti'al form, as is the original form.

Interrogative of magnification and amazement, meaning: they were of a dreadful manner that description cannot encompass. "Nudhur" (warnings) is a verbal noun like "indhar" (warning). It is also said to be the plural of "nadhir" (warner) in the sense of "indhar." Some have taken it to mean "mundhar" (the one warned), but this is worthless; likewise it has been taken to mean "mundhir" (the one warning).

It could be that the verb is "kana" as a complete verb (ناقصة)? Let me translate precisely instead:

It is possible that (kana) is a defective (naqisa, linking) verb, so that "kayfa" is in the position of the predicate (khabar); and that it is a complete verb (tamma), so that "kayfa" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy﴾ ... etc. is an oath clause (*jumla qasamiyya*). It occurs at the end of the four stories, confirming the content of what preceded it in His words ﴿And there had certainly come to them﴾ ... etc., and drawing attention to the fact that each of these stories is independently sufficient to necessitate remembrance and to be an adequate deterrent. Nevertheless, no lesson was drawn from them. That is: "By Allah, We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for your people, by sending it down in their language, filling it with all kinds of admonitions and lessons, and varying within it the threats and promises, ﴿for remembrance﴾, i.e., for taking heed and being admonished. ﴿So is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ is a denial and negation of anyone who heeds, in the most emphatic and forceful form, indicating that no one can answer the questioner with 'yes.'"

It was also said that the meaning is: We made the Qur'an easy for memorization, because of its fine composition, smooth wording, noble and sound meanings, and its freedom from strange (*wahshi*) and similar expressions. Therefore it has an attachment to hearts and a sweetness to the ear. So is there anyone who seeks to memorize it, so that he may be helped in doing so? For this reason Ibn Jubayr said: "No part of the divine books has been memorized by heart except the Qur'an."

Ibn al-Mundhir and a group (of narrators) related from Mujahid that he said: "*Yassarna al-Qur'an* (We made the Qur'an easy): We made its recitation simple."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas: "Had Allah not made it easy upon the tongues of the children of Adam, none of creation would have been able to speak the speech of Allah, the Exalted."

Al-Daylami related from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar to this.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Sirin that he passed by a man who was saying "*surah khafifa*" (a light surah). He said: "Do not say that; rather say '*surah yasira*' (an easy surah), because Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance﴾."

The meaning mentioned first is more suitable to the context. Perhaps the report from Anas, if it is authentic, is not an explanation of the verse. It has also been permitted to interpret *yassarna* as *hayya'na* (We prepared), from their saying "*yassara naqatahu li-l-safar*" (he prepared his she-camel for the journey) when he saddled it, and "*yassara farasahu li-l-ghazw*" (he prepared his horse for the raid) when he saddled and bridled it. The poet said:

*"And I stood up to him with the bridle, prepared; there he will repay me for what I used to do."*

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 54, verse 18:

﴿كَذَّبَتْ عادٌ﴾ ("The people of ʿAd denied") marks the beginning of a new story, and it is not joined by a conjunction (waw of coordination). Likewise the stories that follow it are not joined, which indicates that each story is independent in its purpose and in the lesson it carries. Since the people of Noah had no proper name (ʿalam), they were mentioned with an idafa construction (i.e., "the people of Noah"). Since the people of Hud had a proper name, which is ʿAd, they were mentioned by it, because it is more eloquent in definiteness. The meaning is that ʿAd denied Hud, peace be upon him, and the text does not address the manner of their denial of him, peace be upon him, for the sake of brevity and in haste to state what contains the warning of the punishment. As for His saying: ﴿فَكَيْفَ كانَ عَذابِي ونُذُرِ﴾ ("So how was My punishment and My warnings?"), it serves to direct the hearts of the listeners to attend to what is about to be conveyed to them before it is mentioned, not to magnify or exalt it, nor to make them marvel at its state after its explanation, as is the case with what comes before and after it. It is as if it were said: "ʿAd denied; so have you heard, or listen: how was My punishment and My warning to them?" It has also been said that it is for magnification too, because of the strangeness of what they were punished with, namely the wind, and its being singular in this kind of punishment. But there is a point to be examined in this.

(p. 85)

Allah's words, ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a furious wind﴾, are a resumed clause explaining what was stated in summary earlier. *Sarsar* means cold, according to what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, and al-Dahhak. It was also said to mean one with a violent sound. The full discussion has already passed in *Fussilat*.

﴿On a day of ill omen﴾, a calamity upon them, ﴿continuous﴾. That ill omen was continuous, because after they were destroyed they continued to be punished in *al-barzakh* (the intermediate state between death and resurrection) until they enter Hell on the Day of Resurrection. The word "day" here refers to time in general, based on Allah's words, ﴿So We sent upon them a furious wind on days of ill omen﴾ [Fussilat: 16], and His words, ﴿He subjected it against them for seven nights and eight days in succession﴾ [al-Haqqah: 7]. It is well known that the day was Wednesday, and that it was the last Wednesday of Shawwal, in the sense that the sending of the wind began on it. This does not contradict the two verses of *Fussilat* and *al-Haqqah*.

It has been permitted that *mustamirr* (continuous) be an attribute of "day," meaning: on a day that continued against them until it destroyed them, or that included their elders and their young, until no living soul remained among them. The continuity may be in terms of time or in terms of persons and individuals. However, on the first reading there must be a figurative usage, either by meaning the continuance of its ill omen, or by taking "day" to mean time in general, because a single day does not continue. So reflect on this. It has also been permitted that *mustamirr* means firm, or that it means very bitter, figuratively for its horror and severity of terror, since it has no pleasant taste. It has also been permitted that it be a substitute (*badal*) or an appositive (*'atf bayan*), but as you see, that is not the case. Al-Hasan read *yawmin nahisin* with tanwin on *yawm* and a kasrah on the *ha'* of *nahs*, making it an attribute of *yawm*, so that *mustamirr* is necessarily a second attribute. Some have supported this with what Waki' in *al-Gharar*, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Khatib al-Baghdadi transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas as *marfu'* (traced to the Prophet ﷺ): "The last Wednesday of the month is a continuous ill-omened day." Many people acted on this, considered it an omen, and abandoned their affairs on that day, saying: "Wednesday, it does not turn," and on this is the verse:

"Your meeting with the early riser is an evil omen, and your face, O Wednesday that does not turn."

This is not appropriate. The hadith mentioned has in its chain Maslamah ibn al-Salt, of whom Abu Hatim said: "abandoned" (*matruk*). Ibn al-Jawzi definitively ruled it fabricated. Ibn Rajab said: "a hadith that is not authentic, and its attribution to the Prophet is not agreed upon, for al-Tuyuri transmitted it by another route as *mawquf* (ending with Ibn 'Abbas)." al-Sakhawi said: "all its routes are weak." They also declared weak the report of al-Tabarani: "Wednesday is a continuous ill-omened day." The meaning of the verse is already known. Reports and narrations have come that indicate its praise. In *Minhaj* by al-Halimi and *Shu'ab al-Iman* by al-Bayhaqi, it is said that supplication is answered on Wednesday after midday. Burhan al-Islam mentioned in *Ta'lim al-Muta'allim* from the author of *al-Hidayah*: "Nothing begun on Wednesday was ever left incomplete, and it is the day on which Allah created light." Therefore a group of scholars would seek to begin teaching on that day. Some recommended planting trees on it, based on the report of Ibn Hayyan and al-Daylami from Jabir as *marfu'*: "Whoever plants trees on Wednesday and says: 'Glory be to the Originator, the Inheritor,' its fruit will come to him." Yet there are also reports and narrations indicating the opposite. In *al-Firdaws* from 'A'ishah as *marfu'*: "Were it not that I would dislike for my Ummah, I would have ordered them not to travel on Wednesday. The most beloved days to me for setting out are Thursday." This is not known to be authentic in my view.

Abu Ya'la transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn 'Adi and Tammam in his *Fawa'id* from Abu Sa'id as *marfu'*: "Saturday is a day of deceit and trickery; Sunday is a day of planting and building; Monday is a day of travel and seeking provision; Tuesday is a day of iron and violence; Wednesday is a day of neither taking nor giving; Thursday is a day of seeking needs and entering upon the ruler; and Friday is a day of sermon and marriage." al-Sakhawi criticized this, saying its chain is weak. Ibn Majah transmitted from Ibn 'Umar as *marfu'*, and al-Hakim narrated it by two other routes: "Leprosy and vitiligo appear only on Wednesday." Some reports say it is forbidden to cut nails on Wednesday, and that this causes vitiligo. Some scholars disliked visiting the sick on it, and on this someone said:

"No sick person came on a Wednesday, except we buried him on Thursday."

It is also related that one of them said to his brother: "Come out with me on an errand." He said: "It is Wednesday." He said: "Yunus (Jonah) was born on it." He said: "Indeed, his blessing has become evident in the spaciousness of his place and the goodness of his clothing, until Allah delivered him." He said: "Yusuf (Joseph), peace be upon him, was also born on it." He said: "How well his brothers did to him, until his imprisonment and estrangement lasted long." He said: "On it also was the victory of the Chosen One, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, on the day of the Confederates." He said: "Indeed, but that was after the eyes had turned away and the hearts had reached the throats."

al-Manawi quoted from *al-Bahr* that the Prophet's ﷺ report about the ill omen of the last Wednesday of the month is a matter of *tayarah* (taking omens), which is a practice of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance), since it is not part of the religion. Nor is it based on the view of the astrologers that it is the day of Mercury, which is an ill omen among the ill omens, and fortune among the fortunes, for that is a false statement. It may be that it is a matter of warning and caution, meaning: beware of that day because of what descended on it of punishment and what destruction occurred in it, and renew your repentance to Allah Most High on it, fearing that misfortune may befall you on it as it befell those before you. This is like what he said when he came to al-Hijr: "Do not enter upon these punished people unless you are weeping." And other such things.

It is also related that one of them said: "Taking omens is disliked by a legal (*shar'iyyah*) dislike. However, the Law permits anyone who has an affair of his interests on the last Wednesday to leave acting upon it, not by way of omen-taking and believing that it harms or benefits without Allah's permission, but by way of believing it permissible to refrain on it for what the soul dislikes, not following omen-taking, but affirming the concession to avoid it for whoever wishes, along with the obligation to believe that nothing harms anything." It is transmitted from al-Halimi that he said: "We know from the explanation of the Law that some days are ill-omened, and their opposite is fortune. If the first is established, the second is also established. Thus some days are ill-omened and some are fortunate, just as some people are wretched and some are blessed. But it is claimed that days and stars make people ill-fated or fortunate by choosing times and persons, and this is false. As for the statement that the stars may be causes for good and evil, benefit and harm, while all is the action of Allah alone, there is no harm in that."

Then al-Manawi said: "The conclusion is that avoiding Wednesday by way of omen-taking, or with the belief of the astrologers, is forbidden, with a severe prohibition, for all days belong to Allah Most High; they neither benefit nor harm by their own essence. Without that belief there is no harm or prohibition in it. Whoever takes omens, its ill fortune befalls him. Whoever is certain that none harms or benefits except Allah, Mighty and Majestic, nothing of that affects him, as it was said:

'Know that there is no omen, except upon the one who takes omens, and that is destruction.'"

End of quote. I say: All days are equal, and there is no particular distinction for Wednesday. No hour of the hours is anything but fortunate for one person and ill-omened for another, in terms of what Allah Most High brings about in it of the agreeable and the disagreeable, the good and the evil. So every day has both qualities, according to the different viewpoints. Even if Wednesday is considered ill-omened because some event occurred on it, then every day should be considered ill-omened, for night enters into day and day into night only for the bringing forth of events. And it has been said:

"Indeed the days are sons of one father, and these nights are all sisters."

It is related that the punishment came upon Thamud in the morning of Sunday. It has also been narrated, though I do not think it is authentic: "We seek refuge in Allah Most High from the Day of Sunday, for it has an edge sharper than the sword." Even if it were authentic, perhaps it refers to a particular Sunday whose events were known by revelation. Some claimed that it is a tested matter, recorded always, that whenever the fourteenth day of the lunar month falls on Sunday and something is done on it, it does not succeed. This is not accepted.

It is recorded in *al-Firdaws* from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud: "Allah Most High created diseases on Tuesday, and on it He sent Iblis down to the earth, and on it He created Hell, and on it Allah Most High gave the Angel of Death power over the souls of the children of Adam. On it Qabil killed Habil, on it Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both, died, and on it Ayyub was tested." This hadith, if authentic, does not indicate its ill omen. At most, what happened on it happened, and other good things also occurred on it. In the narration of Muslim: "al-Manfa' was created on Tuesday," meaning that by which livelihood is sustained. If you search the histories, you will come upon great events on all other days. It suffices in this matter that the event of 'Ad encompassed the days of the week, for He, glorified is He, said: ﴿He subjected it against them for seven nights and eight days in succession﴾ [al-Haqqah: 7]. So if ill fortune is for that reason, then tell me: which day of the week was free of it?!

In my view, similar to the matter of ill fortune is the matter of assigning each day a particular task, as many people claim. They cite in that verses that al-Hafiz al-Dimyati attributed to 'Ali, may Allah honor his face:

"So excellent is Saturday, truly, for hunting, if you wish, without doubt. On Sunday is building, for in it God manifested Himself in creating the heavens. On Monday, if you travel, you will return with success and wealth. Whoever wishes cupping, then Tuesday, for in its hours is the shedding of blood. If a man drinks medicine on a day, then excellent is Wednesday. On Thursday is the fulfilling of a pilgrim's need, for Allah permits fulfillment. On Fridays are marriage and wedding and the pleasures of men with women. And this knowledge none knows except a prophet or the successor of the prophets."

I do not think these are authentic. My final word is: what Allah wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be. Time has no influence in this, nor anything else. Some times have a distinction that cannot be denied, like Friday, the month of Ramadan, and others. Some times have the opposite, like the times when prayer is disliked. But this is a matter, and the point of dispute is a matter. So keep this in mind. And may Allah Most High guide you.

Allah's words, ﴿pulling people out﴾, may be an attribute (ṣifah) of the wind, or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from it, because it has been described and so has come close to being definite. It is also permissible that it be a resumptive new sentence (mustaʾnaf). The word "people" (al-nās) is used instead of a pronoun referring to ʿĀd, and it is said this was to include both their males and their females. Al-nazʿ means uprooting. It is narrated that they entered the ravines and the pits, and some of them clung to others, and the wind uprooted them and felled them dead.

﴿As if they were trunks of uprooted palm trees﴾, that is, uprooted from their places and fallen on the ground. It is said they were likened to aʿjāz al-nakhl, which are its roots without branches, because the wind would pull up their heads, so they remained bodies and trunks without heads. This comparison is made more beautiful by the fact that they were people of large, tall bodies. Al-nakhl (palm trees) is a collective noun which is treated as masculine when considering the wording, as here, and as feminine when considering the meaning, as in His words, ﴿trunks of hollow palm trees﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah 69:7]. Treating each in its own way in each of the two places is for the sake of the verse-ending (fāṣilah). The simile clause is a circumstantial clause from "people", and it is a presumed circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddarah). Al-Ṭabarī said: there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the estimate is "so He left them as if they were...", so the kāf, according to what is in al-Baḥr, is in the accusative position governed by the omitted element, but this is not the best view.

Abū Nuhayk read aʿjuz on the pattern of afʿal, like ḍabʿ and aḍbuʿ. His words, ﴿So how was My punishment and My warnings?﴾, are an expression of awe at both of them and of wonder at their situation after their explanation, so there is no trace of repetition with what came before. It is said that the first refers to what befell them in this world, and the second to what will befall them in the Hereafter. The word "kāna" (was) is used for the sake of harmony (mushākalah), or to indicate the certainty of its occurrence, in accordance with His, glorified is He, customary manner in His reports. It was objected that placing the second upon the worldly punishment rules this out.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 54, verse 22–23:

﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember?﴾ The discussion regarding it is like that which has passed. ﴿Thamud denied the warners.﴾ That is, the messengers, upon them be peace. For the denial of one of them, namely Salih, peace be upon him, here amounts to denial of all of them, because they agree upon the fundamentals of the sharia (shara'i'). It is also permissible that "al-nudhur" be a verbal noun (masdar), or a plural of it, and that it be the plural of "nadhir" in the sense of "one warned by it" (al-mundhar minhu). So do not be heedless.
