Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 54, verse 24:

﴿Then they said: "Shall we follow a single human being from among us?"﴾ That is, one who is of our own kind (kā'inan min jinsinā), the prepositional phrase (al-jār wa'l-majrūr) being in the position of a qualifier (ṣifah) of "basharan" (a human being). Its accusative case (intiṣābuhu) is governed by a verb that is explained by the following "nattabi'u" (we follow), meaning: "Shall we follow a human being?" ﴿single﴾ means alone, having no followers; or [it means] one of their individuals, not one of their nobles, as is understood from the indefiniteness (al-tankīr), which indicates non-specification. It is another qualifier of "basharin." Its being placed after the first qualifier, despite the latter being in the form of a prepositional phrase (shibh al-jumlah), serves to draw attention to the fact that both belonging to their kind (al-jinsiyyah) and being singular (al-waḥdah) prevent following him; had it been placed before the first, this admonition would have been lost. Abu al-Sammal read, as reported by al-Hudhali in his book al-Kamil, and Abu 'Amr al-Dani [read]: "a-basharun minnā wāḥidun" with both in the nominative case, on the basis that "basharun" is the subject (mubtada'), and what follows is its qualifier, and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿nattabi'uhu﴾ is its predicate (khabar). Ibn Khalawayh, the author of al-Lawami', and Ibn 'Atiyyah transmitted from Abu al-Sammal the nominative "basharun" and the accusative "wāḥidan." Ibn 'Atiyyah explained this as follows: the nominative of "basharun" is either by supposing a verb in the passive voice, the implied sense being "ayunabba'u basharun" (is a human being informed?), or by way of the inceptive (ibtida'), with the predicate being the clause ﴿nattabi'uhu﴾. The accusative of "wāḥidan" is as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), either from the pronoun of accusative in ﴿nattabi'uhu﴾ or from the pronoun that is resident in "minnā." The author of al-Lawami' also explained the accusative of "wāḥidan" in this way, and as for the nominative of "basharin," he explained it as an inceptive with an omitted predicate, meaning: "a-basharun minnā yubda'u ilaynā aw yursalu aw naḥwuhumā" (Is a human being from among us sent to us, or dispatched, or the like?). The preceding interrogative favours assuming a verb which takes "basharun" as its agent. ﴿Indeed we, then﴾ means: if we follow a single human being from among us, ﴿are surely in error﴾, a great straying from the truth, ﴿and madness﴾, that is, fires; "su'ur" is the plural of "sa'ir" (blaze).

It is reported that Salih, peace be upon him, used to say to them: "If you do not follow me, you will be in error from the truth and in madness." So they reversed the statement against him, out of extremity of their rebelliousness, saying: "If we follow you, we will indeed be as you say." Thus the speech is of the type of inversion (min bāb al-ta'kīs) and the statement "bi'l-mūjib" (answering according to the implication). The plural "su'ur" is in view of the levels (al-darakāt) [of Hell], or for emphasis (lil-mubālaghah). It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas something that can bear what we have said, for he said: "i.e., they are in distance from the truth and in punishment." In another narration from him, "su'ur" is explained as madness, as a singular noun with that meaning; it is said: "a she-camel that is mad-ridden (masʿūrah)" when she exceeds in her pace as if she were mad. The poet said:

"As if within her were a madness, when the camels are stirred by a quick trot and a slackening of the march, wearying."

The first interpretation is more correct and more eloquent.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 54, verse 25:

﴿Has the Reminder been cast upon him from among us?﴾ That is: has the revelation been sent down to him from among us, while among us there is one who is more deserving of it than he is? The use of the verb "ulqiya" (was cast) rather than "unzila" (was sent down) is said to be because it carries the sense of haste in the act. ﴿Rather, he is a liar, an insolent one.﴾ That is, excessively arrogant (ashir, from al-ashar, "exultant, insolent pride"). According to al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani), it is a bewilderment that befalls a person from poor endurance of a blessing, from failing to fulfil its due and from placing it other than where it belongs. Close to it is tarab (exhilaration), which is a lightness that most often befalls one from joy. Their meaning is: the matter is not as they say, rather he is such-and-such, whose excessive arrogance and desire for prominence over them led him to claim that. Qatadah and Abu Qilabah recited ﴿Rather, he is the liar, the insolent one﴾ with the definite article (al-) in both words and with a fatha on the shin and a shadda on the ra', and what is to be said about that will come shortly, God willing.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 54, verse 26:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They will know tomorrow who is the liar, the insolent one﴾, is a relating of what He, glorified and exalted, said to Salih, upon him be peace, as a promise to him and a warning to his people. The sin (sin) here serves to bring the content of the sentence near and to emphasize it. By "tomorrow" is meant the time of the descent of the worldly punishment upon them. It was also said: it is the Day of Resurrection, so it refers to unrestricted future time, and it was expressed with it to bring it near. In support of this is the verse of al-Tirimmah:

Ala 'allilani qabla nawh al-nawa'ih
wa qabla idtirab al-nafs bayn al-jawanih

wa qabla ghadin ya lahfa nafsi 'ala ghad
idha raha ashabi wa lastu bi-ra'ih

That is: ﴿They will know﴾ certainly, in the near future, ﴿who is the liar, the insolent one﴾, the one whose insolence and arrogance led him to what led him: is it Salih, or the one who denied him? The intended meaning is that they will know that they themselves are the liars and the insolent ones, but it was presented in the form of ambiguity to indicate that this is something that is hardly hidden. Similar to it is the saying of the poet:

Fa-la'in laqaytuka khaliyayni li-ta'lamanna
ayyi wa ayyuka faris al-ahzab

Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, Talhah, Ibn Thabbab and al-A'mash read "ta'lamun" (you will know) with the second-person prefix, as a relating of what Salih said to them in answer to them. In al-Kashshaf: "or it is a statement by way of iltifat (shift of address)." The author of al-Kashf said: that is, it is the speech of God, exalted, to the people of Thamud by way of iltifat toward them, either in His address to Our Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, and this is similar to what He related about Shu'ayb: ﴿So he turned away from them and said, "O my people, I had certainly conveyed to you"﴾ [al-A'raf: 93], after they had been utterly destroyed. It is an eloquent speech, in which there is an indication that they deserve this warning, and as if they were present in the assembly, and He turned the face toward them to rebuke them for their crimes. Or it is in His address, exalted and majestic, to Salih, upon him be peace, and the revelation is a relating of that speech which contains the iltifat. On both assumptions there is no difficulty in it, as was imagined, and al-Zamakhshari's wording on the first is more indicative and more eloquent. End. As for one who considers what the majority said about iltifat, I do not think his soul would be at rest with what was mentioned, so reflect.

Mujahid, as reported by the author of al-Lawami' and Abu Qays al-Awdi, read "al-Ushur" with three damm (u-vowels) and a light ra. It is said: ashir and ushur, like hadhir and hudhur, so the damma on the shin is a dialect form and the damma on the hamza follows it. Al-Kisa'i related from Mujahid the damma on the shin without the hamza, so it is like nadus.

Abu Haywa read "al-ashharr" as an elative (af'al al-tafdil), meaning the more emphatic in wickedness. Likewise Qatadah and Abu Qilabah read it, though its usage is rare, even if it is according to the original form, like al-akhir in the verse of Ru'bah:

Bilal khayr al-nas wa ibn al-akhyar

Abu Hatim said: the Arabs hardly speak with "al-akhyar" and "al-ashharr" except in poetic necessity, and he recited the verse. Al-Jawhari said: "al-ashharr" is only said in a poor dialect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 54, verse 31:

﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a single shout﴾ It was the shout of Jibril (peace be upon him), who cried out at dawn on Sunday, as al-Manawi related from al-Zamakhshari, at the edge of their dwellings. ﴿So they became﴾, i.e., they turned into ﴿like the crushed stalks of the one who makes an enclosure﴾, i.e., like dry vegetation that the owner of a pen (ḥazīrah) gathers for his livestock in winter.

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit), al-Hashim (hashīm) is what has been crushed and broken into pieces from trees. (And al-Muḥtaẓir) is the one who builds the enclosure, for parts of what he works with crumble off of him during the work and fall away. Or al-Hashim may be what has dried out from the enclosure over a long time, trampled by animals so that it breaks apart. This was objected to, on the grounds that the more apparent reading is "like the crushed stalks of the enclosure," and the ḥazīrah is the pen that the Arabs construct. The people of the desert [build] for their livestock and shelter from branches, leafy trees and reeds, from ḥaẓr (ḥaẓr), which means prevention.

Al-Hasan, Abu Ḥaywah, Abu al-Sammal, Abu Rajaʾ and ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd read «al-Muḥtaẓar» with a fatḥah on the ẓāʾ, as an ism of place (ism makān), and the intended meaning is the enclosure itself; or it is an ism of the object (ism mafʿūl). It has been said that a noun is to be supplied to it, i.e., (like the crushed stalks of the enclosed wall); or nothing is supplied, on the basis that al-Muḥtaẓar is the pen itself, as you have heard. It is also permitted that it be a verbal noun (maṣdar), i.e., like the crushed stalks of enclosing, i.e., what crumbled during the act of enclosing.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 54, verses 32–33:

And His saying, ﴿They denied all Our signs﴾, is a resumptive sentence (*istiʾnaf*, a new sentence that answers an implied question) arising from the narration of the coming of the warners, as if it were said: "What then did the people of Pharaoh do at that time?" It was said in reply: they denied all of Our signs, which are the signs of all the prophets, peace be upon them, for denying some of them is denying all of them. Or the signs are the nine signs. Al-Wahidi permitted that by "the warners" is meant the signs themselves. Thus His words, glorified is He, ﴿with Our signs﴾ are an instance of placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun, the original being "they denied them." Some of the extreme Shiites, who in our time are called the Kashfiyya, claim that by "all the signs" is meant ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, because he is the "clear register" mentioned in His saying, ﴿And everything We have enumerated in a clear register﴾ [Yā-Sīn 36:12], and that he, may Allah ennoble his face, appeared with Moses, peace be upon him, before Pharaoh and his people, but they did not believe. This is among the nonsense in abundance. We ask Allah, exalted is He, for pardon and well-being. ﴿So We seized them﴾, that is, the people of Pharaoh. Some claimed that the pronoun in ﴿they denied﴾ and the pronoun in "We seized them" refer to all the nations previously mentioned, and that the speech is complete at His saying, ﴿the warners﴾. This is not correct. The fāʾ is for consequence: ﴿So We seized them﴾ and overpowered them because of their denial, ﴿with the seizing of the Mighty﴾ who cannot be overcome, ﴿the Omnipotent﴾ whom nothing can frustrate. The word "seizing" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*, an absolute object), not as a simile (*tashbīh*). ﴿Are your disbelievers better than those?﴾, that is, the disbelievers enumerated: the people of Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, and the people of Pharaoh. The superiority meant is in terms of the world and its adornments, such as the abundance of strength and might, and the great number of troops and equipment. Or it is in terms of the softness of their obstinacy in disbelief, so that the disbelievers addressed here are less stubborn and nearer to obedience and submission. The apparent meaning of the words of many is that the address here is general to the Muslims and others, since they said:

[p. 92]

﴿Are your disbelievers, O company of Arabs, better than...﴾ etc. The interrogative is one of denial (istifham inkari), so the sense is: "Your disbelievers are not better than those disbelievers who were counted (before you), in that they were stronger and more powerful and greater in number and equipment, or in that they were more pliant in disbelief, rebellion, misguidance and transgression. Rather, they are inferior to them in strength and what resembles it of the adornments of the world, or worse off than them in disbelief. And one who was better than you was struck by punishment, so how can they hope that the like will not befall them?" Similarly, it has been said regarding the address in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Or do you have an exemption in the scriptures?﴾, that the phrase is taken as being governed by the implied "am" (or) applying to "your disbelievers." This is a turning away (idrab) and a transition to another rebuke, as if it were said: "Rather, do your disbelievers have an exemption and security from the consequences of what they do of disbelief and sins and their ruinous outcomes in the heavenly books? Therefore they persist in what they are upon and do not fear." Some scholars chose in this matter that the address is specific to the disbelievers. And regarding His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Or do they say: We are a united host, victorious?﴾, they said it is a turning away from the aforementioned rebuke to another rebuke, by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), to signal that their state leads to their being turned away from and dropped from the rank of direct address, and to relate their ugly deeds to others.

That is: "Rather, do they say, confident in their power: We are a group whose affair is unified, which cannot be attacked or oppressed?" Or ﴿victorious﴾ means one who is victorious over enemies and cannot be overcome; or "mutually supportive," each of us supporting the others.

In the view of this humble servant, what is preponderant is that the address in both places is specific, as the context requires, to the disbelievers of Makkah or the Arabs. This is apparent in the second place and needs nothing further. As for the first place, its justification is that the construction be like the idafa in "all the dirhams are so-and-so," and "the Tur of Sinai," and "the day of Sunday." He did not say "Are you...?" in order to explicitly identify their disbelief, which requires their destruction. It is also possible that in ﴿Are your disbelievers...﴾ there is a kind of tajrid (abstraction) which they mentioned in cases like ﴿For them therein is the abode of eternity﴾ [Fussilat: 28], as if some disbelievers were abstracted from them and then attributed to them. There is in this as much exaggeration as there is. It is also possible that this is a reason for deviating from "Are you...?" And perhaps what makes preponderant that the negated superiority is considered in terms of their pliancy in disbelief is that, when Glorified is He frightened the disbelievers who denied the signs and turned away from them, saying they are "continuous magic," by mentioning what befell the earlier nations, at which the lines of threat tremble and quiver, Mighty and Majestic is He said to them: Why do you not fear that there will befall you the like of what befell them? "Are you less disbelieving and obstinate than them, so that this would be a cause of security from the descent of the like of their punishment upon you? Or has Allah, Mighty and Majestic, given you an exemption from His punishment? Or are you mightier than them, victorious over the armies of Allah, Exalted is He?" Glorified is He deviated from "or are you a united host, victorious" to what is in the sublime arrangement, to indicate that this has no reality at all except by mere utterance and bare claim, which is not agreed upon. So reflect. The secrets of the speech of Allah, Exalted is He, have no end. Then do not hasten to object to what we have said even if we have no predecessor in it, as far as we have searched. Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 54, verse 45:

The words of His, exalted is He: ﴿Their multitude will be routed﴾ are a refutation of their saying that. The *sin* (*sīn*) here is for emphasis, meaning: their multitude will certainly be routed. ﴿And they will turn their backs﴾, that is, *al-adbār* (the backs). It has also been read thus. The singular is used to intend the genus, which applies to many, while observing the rhyme (*fawāṣil*) and the harmony with the surrounding phrases. Or it is because the verb is in the sense of "each one of them will turn his back," following the pattern of: "The amir clothed us with a robe (*kasānā al-amīr ḥullatan*)." This is with the same observance mentioned above as well. This happened on the day of Badr, and it is one of the signs of prophethood (*dalā'il al-nubuwwah*), because the verse is Meccan (*makkiyyah*, revealed in Mecca), and it was revealed at a time when no fighting had been prescribed and no battle had taken place. For this reason, ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "On the day it was revealed, which multitude will be routed?" That is, from among the multitudes of the disbelievers? And no one among them had been mentioned in connection with fighting. The report has already been mentioned.

From what we have pointed to, it is known that al-Tibi's view regarding this narration is questionable, because the interrogative hamza in ﴿Or do they say﴾ etc. shows that the identity of those who will be routed arises from heedlessness of what ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, intended.

Abu Haywa, Musa al-Aswari and Abu al-Barahsam read: *satahzimu al-jam'a* (you will rout the multitude), with a *fatḥah* on the *tā'* and a *kasrah* on the *zāy*, addressed to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, with *al-jam'* in the accusative as the object. Abu Haywa also read, and Ya'qub, *sanahzimu* (we will rout), with an *nūn* that is open and a *kasrah* on the *zāy*, attributing the verb to the pronoun of majesty. And from Abu Haywa and Ibn Abi Abla: *sayahzimu al-jam'a*, with a *fatḥah* on the *yā'*, in the active voice, and *al-jam'* in the accusative, meaning: Allah, exalted is He, will rout the multitude. Abu Haywa and Dawud ibn Abi Salim, from Abu ʿAmr, read: *wa-tuwallūna* (and you will turn), with the *tā'* of address.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 54, verses 46–47:

﴿Nay, the Hour is their appointed time, and the Hour is more calamitous and more bitter.﴾ That is: this is not the full extent of their punishment; rather, the Hour is the appointed time of their torment, and this (worldly punishment) is among its precursors. ﴿And the Hour is more calamitous (adhā)﴾, that is, greater in calamity (dāhiyah), and the dāhiyah is a dreadful, terrible matter from which no way of escape is found. ﴿And more bitter (amarr)﴾, that is, more intense in bitterness to the taste, and this is a metaphor (isti'ārah) for its difficulty upon the soul. It has been said: "more powerful (aqwā)", but this is not the right view. The mention of "the Hour" in the place where a pronoun could have been used is to increase its awe-inspiring effect.

﴿Indeed, the criminals﴾, from the first and the last (generations), ﴿are in error (ḍalāl)﴾, that is, in destruction, ﴿and madness (su'ur)﴾, and blazing fires (nīrān musa''arah). Or: they are in error from the truth, and in fires in the Hereafter. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "in loss and madness."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 54, verse 48:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿On the Day they are dragged into the Fire upon their faces﴾ — i.e., they are dragged (yujarrūn). It is connected to a verb of saying that is understood after it, i.e., "On the Day they are dragged, it will be said to them: ﴿Taste the touch of Saqar﴾." It is also permissible that it be connected to a verb understood from what precedes it, i.e., "they will be punished" or "they will be humiliated" or the like. The clause "it is said" is then a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in (yusḥabūn). It is also permissible that it be connected to "taste" (dhūqū), on the basis that the address is to the deniers addressed in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Are your disbelievers better than those?﴾ and so on. The meaning would be: taste, O deniers of Muhammad (ﷺ), the Day when the guilty predecessors are dragged, and the intended meaning is that they are gathered with them and made equal to them in the Hereafter, just as they harmed them in this world. But this is, as you see, [a weak view].

The intended meaning of "the touch of Saqar" is its pain. This is a metonymy (majāz mursal) in which the cause is mentioned for the effect, since its touch causes the pain of it; and the connection of "tasting" to such a thing is common in usage. In al-Kashshaf: ﴿the touch of Saqar﴾ is like your saying, "he found the touch of fever" and "he tasted the taste of beating," because when the fire reaches them with its heat and afflicts them with its pain, it is as if it touches them with a touch of that kind, just as one touches an animal and makes contact with it in a way that harms and pains. This implies that there is a metaphor by allusion (isti'āra makniyya) in the speech, like His saying, ﴿they break the covenant of God﴾ [al-Ra'd: 25]. It is possible that other than this is intended.

"Saqar" is a proper name for Hell — may God Exalted protect us from it by the blessing of His great speech and the sanctity of His beloved (ḥabīb), upon him be the most excellent prayers and the most complete greetings — derived from "saqartuhu lil-nār" and "ṣaqartuhu" (with the sīn changed to ṣād on account of the qāf), when it scorches him and changes his colour. Dhu al-Rummah, describing a wild bull, said:

When the sun melts, he guards against its scorching heats with branches of a shrub of a level, sparse, thorny patch.

The reason it is not diptote is that it is a proper noun and feminine. ʿAbd Allāh [ibn Masʿūd] read ilā al-nār. Maḥbūb, from Abū ʿAmr, read "massa sSaqar" with the sīn assimilated into the sīn. Ibn Mujāhid criticised this, saying that its assimilation is an error because it is doubled (mushaddad). The assumption about Abū ʿAmr is that he did not assimilate until he deleted one of the two sīns because of the coming together of like letters, and then assimilated.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 54, verse 49:

﴿Indeed, all things﴾ among things, ﴿We created with measure﴾, meaning: decreed and written in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh) before their occurrence. Thus qadar in its well-known sense is what stands opposed to qada' (decree/judgment), and reading the verse in this way is what has been transmitted from many of the early scholars (al-salaf). Imam Ahmad, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The idolaters of Quraysh came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) disputing with him about qadar, and so there was revealed: ﴿On the Day they are dragged into the Fire upon their faces, [it will be said], 'Taste the touch of Saqar.' Indeed, all things We created with measure.﴾"

Al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, Ibn Majah, Ibn 'Adi and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Two groups of my ummah have no share in Islam: the Murji'ah and the Qadariyyah." A verse in the Book of Allah was revealed concerning them: ﴿Indeed, the criminals are in error and madness﴾, to the end of the verses. Ibn 'Abbas used to detest the Qadariyyah greatly. 'Abd ibn Humayd related from Abu Yahya al-A'raj, who said: I heard Ibn 'Abbas, when he mentioned the Qadariyyah, say: "If I were to meet some of them, I would do such-and-such to them," then he said: "Adultery is by qadar, theft is by qadar, and drinking wine is by qadar."

He also related from Mujahid that he said: I said to Ibn 'Abbas: "What do you say about one who denies qadar?" He said: "Bring him together with me." He said: "What would you do with him?" He said: "I would strangle him until I kill him." Their condemnation has come in many hadiths, among them what Ahmad, Abu Dawud and al-Tabarani related from Ibn 'Umar that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every nation has its Magians, and the Magians of my ummah are those who say there is no qadar. If they fall ill, do not visit them, and if they die, do not attend their funerals."

It is also permissible that the meaning is: Indeed, every thing We created is measured, perfected, with the wisdom on which the matter of creation turns. The verse is then in the category of ﴿And He created everything and measured it precisely﴾ [al-Furqan: 2]. ﴿Kulla﴾ (every) is in the accusative, governed by a verb which the following clause explains, meaning: "Indeed We created every thing, We created it." Abu al-Sammal read it in the nominative, and Ibn 'Atiyyah and a group of the People of the Sunnah said: the nominative reading of kulla is by way of the subject (mubtada'), with the clause ﴿khalaqnahu﴾ as the predicate, and ﴿bi-qadar﴾ is attached to it, as in the widely transmitted reading. The verse then also indicates that every thing is created with measure, and it should not be made that the clause ﴿khalaqnahu﴾ is a descriptive qualifier, with ﴿bi-qadar﴾ made the predicate, since the two readings would then differ in meaning, whereas the principle is the agreement of the readings.

Al-Radi said: The meaning does not vary, because God's intention by "every thing" is every created being, whether you put kulla in the accusative or the nominative, and whether you make ﴿khalaqnahu﴾ a qualifier in the nominative case or a predicate about it. This is because "We created every thing with measure" does not mean by it that We created everything that the term "thing" applies to, since He, exalted is He, did not create all the infinite possibilities, while the term "thing" applies to each of them. Then we say: the meaning of ﴿every thing We created with measure﴾, on the reading where ﴿khalaqnahu﴾ is the predicate, is "every created being is with measure," and on the reading where ﴿khalaqnahu﴾ is a qualifier of "every thing," it is "every created thing, existing with measure." The two meanings are one, since the word kulla in the verse is restricted to created beings, whether ﴿khalaqnahu﴾ is a qualifier or a predicate.

This was criticised by al-Sayyid al-Sanad, may his secret be sanctified, who said: If we make ﴿khalaqnahu﴾ a qualifier, the meaning becomes "every created being characterised as being Our creation, existing with measure," and on this, it is not impossible, considering this meaning, that there are created beings not characterised by this attribute, and so they would not fall under the ruling. But if we make it a predicate, or put "every thing" in the accusative, there is no room for this possibility, considering the meaning itself understood from the speech. The two meanings have definitely differed, and it does not benefit him that every created being is in fact characterised by that attribute, because that is understood only from outside the speech, and there is no doubt that what is intended is that meaning which admits of no possibility. Al-Shihab al-Khafaji mentioned something similar. And because the accusative is an explicit text on the intended meaning, the widely transmitted readings agreed upon it, even though it requires an implied element (taqdir); and by this it is preferred over the nominative, which gives an impression of the opposite, even if it does not need that element.

And Our command is but one [act], like a glance of the eye.

Its meaning: Our affair is but a single act, in a manner that does not vary and a mode that does not multiply, namely bringing into being without effort or hardship. Or: Our command is but one word, namely His saying, ﴿Be!﴾ [al-Baqarah: 117], and other than it. The amr (command) is the opposite of the nahy (prohibition) and the singular of al-umur (affairs). So when Almighty and Majestic God wills a thing, He says to it, "Be!" and it is, ﴿like a glance of the eye﴾, that is, in speed and swiftness. It has also been said that this refers to the establishing of the Hour, and it is like His saying, ﴿And the affair of the Hour is but like a glance of the eye﴾ [al-Nahl: 77].

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 54, verse 51:

﴿And We have certainly destroyed your likes﴾, that is, your counterparts in disbelief,

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 54, verse 52:

﴿And every matter they have done﴾ of disbelief and sins. The pronoun in "they have done" (fa'aluhu) refers back to the partisans (al-ashya') (i.e., the previous generations of deniers), as related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. The clause "they have done it" (fa'aluhu) is a qualifying clause (sifah) of "matter" (shay'), and the linking element (al-rabit) is the accusative pronoun (damir al-nasb). His, may He be exalted, words "in the scriptures" (fi al-zubur) are a complement attached to a specific verb of being (kawn khass), serving as the predicate (khabar) of the subject. That is: every matter they did in the world is written in the books of the recording angels (al-hafazah), not neglected. Explaining "the scriptures" (al-zubur) as the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), as al-Tabarsi related it, is not correct.

The readers (al-qurra') did not differ over the nominative reading of "every" (kullu), and the verse is not of the type of al-ishtighal (the construction in which the verb is occupied with a pronoun referring to the preceding noun), so the accusative reading is not permissible. This is because the meaning produced by the nominative would not remain if the verb were applied to the pronoun in the preceding noun, as is required in that construction. The meaning would then become: "They did in the scriptures every matter," if we attach the prepositional phrase to "they did" (ya'alu), and they did not do any of their deeds in the books; rather they did them in their places, and the angels, peace be upon them, wrote them down against them in the books. Or: "They did every matter that is written in the scriptures," if we make the prepositional phrase a qualifier (na't) of "every matter." And although this is a sound meaning, it is contrary to the intended meaning in the nominative reading, which is what has been stated just above.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 54, verse 53:

﴿And every small and great [matter]﴾ among the deeds, as has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others. It is also said: [it means] among them and among everything that will exist until the Day of Resurrection. ﴿Is recorded﴾, i.e., written down and inscribed in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh) with its details. It is derived from al-satr (the line), in the sense of writing; it is said: satartu and istatartu have the same meaning. Al-A'mash, 'Imran and 'Isma from Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "mustatarr" with a shaddah on the ra'. The author of al-Lawami' said: it may be from ta-rra (to sprout), said of plants and a moustache, when it appears; and the meaning is: every small and great thing is manifest in the Tablet, established in it. It may also be from al-istitar (to be written in lines), but the ra' is doubled for pausal use according to the dialect of those who say "Ja'farr" and "yaf'all" with a shaddah in pause; that is, he then applied the pause form to continuous recitation. Its pattern, according to the first explanation, is mustaf'al, and according to the second, mufta'al. When the description of the evil state of the disbelievers was [given] by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the criminals﴾, etc.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 54, verse 54:

Since the passage requires explaining the good state of the believers, so that warning (tarhib) and encouragement (targhib) are balanced, He, glorified is He, first stated what they will have of good condition in summary (ijmal, a concise statement), saying, Mighty is His saying: ﴿Indeed, the righteous﴾, meaning those who guard themselves against disbelief and sins. It has also been said: against disbelief alone.

﴿in gardens﴾ of great standing, ﴿and rivers﴾, meaning rivers likewise. The singular is used because the generic noun suffices, in consideration of the rhyme endings (fawasil, the closing words of verses). It is reported from Ibn Abbas that it is interpreted as "breadth" (si'ah), and he cited as evidence the verse of Labid ibn Rabi'ah, as in al-Durr al-Manthur, or Qays ibn al-Khatib, as in al-Bahr, describing a spear-wound:

*"I held it with my palm, so I widened its gash, so that a standing man can see what lies behind it through it."*

That is, I widened its gash. The breadth is taken to mean the breadth of the dwellings, as is most apparent. It has also been said: the breadth of provision and livelihood. It has also been said: what encompasses both. Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul reported from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said: ﴿and rivers﴾ means in light and radiance. This is a metaphor, comparing the spreading radiance to water flowing forth from its source. It is also permissible that it means "daytime" in its literal sense, and the meaning is that there is no darkness and no night for them in the gardens.

al-A'raj, Mujahid, Humayd, Abu al-Sammal and al-Fayyad ibn Ghazwan read «ونَهْرٍ» with the ha' sukun (silent), and this has the same meaning as «نَهَرٍ» with the ha' fathah (vowelled). al-A'mash, Abu Nuhayk, Abu Mijlaz and al-Yamani read «ونُهُرٍ» with damma on the nun and the ha', and this is the plural of nahr (whether vowelled with fathah or sukun), like asad and usud, and rahn and ruhun. It has been said that it is the plural of nahar (daytime), and the meaning is that there is no darkness and no night for them, as was related earlier. It has also been said: it was read with damma on the nun and sukun on the ha'.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 54, verse 55:**

﴿In a seat of truth﴾: in a pleasing place. Some hold that "truth" is a *majaz mursal* (figurative usage through a related meaning, here a necessary attribute) or an *isti'arah* (metaphor). It has also been said that the intended meaning is the truth of the one promised, who is Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ). Or the meaning is that whoever attains it attains it through his truthfulness and his affirmation of the Messengers (peace be upon them), so the idafah (genitive construction) is for the most remote connection. Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: He praised the place with truth, so only the people of truth sit in it. It is the seat in which Allah makes true His promises to His friends, that He, Glorified and Exalted, will permit them to gaze upon His Noble Face. The singular *maq'ad* is used to indicate the category (*jins*).

Uthman al-Batti read *fi maqa'id* (in seats), in the plural, and this clarifies that the intended meaning of *maq'ad* is the seats. ﴿Near a Sovereign﴾: that is, a King of great dominion. It is an intensive form (*sighat mubalaghah*), and the yā' is not from *ishba'* (vowel lengthening). ﴿All-Powerful﴾: Capable, of great power. The adverbial phrase (*zarf*) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relative to the pronoun resting in the prepositional phrase, or it is a predicate after a predicate, or a qualifier of *maq'ad sidq*, or a substitute (*badal*) for it. The "nearness" (*'indiyyah*) denotes nearness of rank (*qurb rutbi*).

Some scholars have said that He, Glorified be He, left the nearness and the closeness unspecified, and left *Malik* (Sovereign) and *Muqtadir* (All-Powerful) indefinite, to indicate that the human intellects cannot grasp the reality of His dominion and His power, Exalted is He, and that their nearness to Him, Glorified be He, is of a station of happiness and honour such that "no eye has seen, no ear has heard" of what is beyond description and what the minds fail to conceive.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi narrated from Buraydah (ﷺ), "from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the righteous﴾, etc., he said: The people of Paradise enter upon the Almighty every day twice, and He recites the Qur'an to them, while each man among them is seated in his seat, which is his seat upon pulpits of pearls, rubies, emeralds, gold and silver, according to their deeds. Their eyes are never more delighted than by that, and they have never heard anything greater or better than it. Then they return to their dwellings, their eyes comforted, delighting in the like of it the next day." And if this is sound, then it is among the *mutashabih* (ambiguous verses), like the verse, so do not be heedless. These two magnificent names have a particular significance in the answering of supplication, as in some reports.

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, who said: I entered the mosque thinking that it was morning, but then I found that a long night was over me, with no one in it besides me. So I slept, and I heard a movement behind me, and I was frightened. He said: "O you whose heart is filled with fear, do not be afraid or be alarmed, and say: O Allah, You are the Sovereign, the All-Powerful; whatever You will of matter comes to be. Then ask whatever you wish." He said: So I did not ask Allah, Exalted is He, for anything except that He answered me, and I was saying: O Allah, You are the Sovereign, the All-Powerful; whatever You will of matter comes to be. So grant me happiness in both abodes, be for me and not against me, help me against whoever oppresses me, and protect me from the burden of debt, the subjugation of men, and the mockery of enemies. And send blessings, O Allah, upon our master Muhammad, and upon his family and companions. And all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
